rows.stem:
Let R be a relation in the set N given by

\(R = \{(a, b) : a = b - 2, b > 6\}\).

Then
rows.solution: A pair \((a, b)\) belongs to R only if BOTH conditions hold: \(b > 6\) and \(a = b - 2\). Test each choice. For \((6, 8)\): \(b = 8 > 6\) and \(b - 2 = 6 = a\), so both hold. For \((8, 7)\): \(b = 7 > 6\), but \(b - 2 = 5 \ne 8\). For \((3, 8)\): \(b = 8 > 6\), but \(b - 2 = 6 \ne 3\). For \((2, 4)\): \(b = 4\), which already fails \(b > 6\). Hence the only pair in R is \((6, 8)\).

rows.stem: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & x \\ y & 0 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(A = A^T\), where \(A^T\) is the transpose of the matrix A, then
rows.solution: Transposing swaps the off-diagonal entries: \(A^T = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & y \\ x & 0 \end{bmatrix}\). The condition \(A = A^T\) says A is symmetric, so compare entries position by position. The \((1,1)\) and \((2,2)\) entries agree automatically; the \((1,2)\) entries give \(x = y\) and the \((2,1)\) entries give \(y = x\), which is the same condition. So the only requirement is \(x = y\) — no particular numerical values are forced, which is why the choices fixing \(x\) and \(y\) separately, or fixing their sum, are not implied.

The angle \(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\) lies in the second quadrant, where the cosine is negative: \(\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{4} = -\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4} = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\). Taking the modulus, \(f\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right) = \left|-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right| = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\). A modulus can never be negative, so the two negative choices are ruled out on sight, and \(1\) is impossible because \(|\cos x| = 1\) only at integer multiples of \(\pi\). Hence the value is \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\).

rows.stem: The function \(f(x) = x^3 + 3x\) is increasing in interval
rows.solution: Differentiating, \(f'(x) = 3x^2 + 3 = 3(x^2 + 1)\). Since \(x^2 \ge 0\) for every real \(x\), we get \(f'(x) \ge 3 > 0\) at every point, so \(f\) is increasing on the whole real line. The other three choices are each only a part of the real line; \(f\) does increase on them too, but the complete interval of increase — and so the correct description — is R.

rows.subtopic: Order and Degree of a Differential Equation
rows.stem: The order and the degree of the differential equation \(\left(1 + 3\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^2 = 4\dfrac{d^3y}{dx^3}\) respectively are :
rows.solution: The equation is already polynomial in the derivatives; expanding the left side gives \(1 + 6\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 9\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^2 = 4\dfrac{d^3y}{dx^3}\). The ORDER is the order of the highest derivative present, namely \(\dfrac{d^3y}{dx^3}\), so the order is 3. The DEGREE is the power to which that highest derivative is raised once the equation is polynomial in derivatives; here \(\dfrac{d^3y}{dx^3}\) occurs to the first power, so the degree is 1. The exponent 2 on the left belongs to \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\), not to the highest derivative, and so plays no part in the degree — which is the trap the choices are built around. Hence the order and degree are 3 and 1.

Write \(\vec{a} = a_1\hat{i} + a_2\hat{j} + a_3\hat{k}\) and take the three dot products in turn. From \(\vec{a} \cdot \hat{i} = 1\) we get \(a_1 = 1\). From \(\vec{a} \cdot (\hat{i} + \hat{j}) = 1\) we get \(a_1 + a_2 = 1\), so \(a_2 = 0\). From \(\vec{a} \cdot (\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}) = 1\) we get \(a_1 + a_2 + a_3 = 1\), so \(a_3 = 0\). Hence \(\vec{a} = \hat{i}\).

rows.stem:
Find the value of k for which the function f given as

\(f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1 - \cos x}{2x^2}, & \text{if } x \ne 0 \\ k, & \text{if } x = 0 \end{cases}\) is continuous at \(x = 0\).
rows.solution: Continuity at \(x = 0\) requires \(\lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = f(0) = k\), so the whole job is to evaluate the limit. Use \(1 - \cos x = 2\sin^2\dfrac{x}{2}\). For \(x \ne 0\), \(f(x) = \dfrac{1 - \cos x}{2x^2} = \dfrac{2\sin^2\dfrac{x}{2}}{2x^2} = \dfrac{\sin^2\dfrac{x}{2}}{x^2}\). Since \(x = 2 \cdot \dfrac{x}{2}\), we have \(x^2 = 4\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^2\), so \(f(x) = \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\dfrac{\sin\dfrac{x}{2}}{\dfrac{x}{2}}\right)^2\). As \(x \to 0\) the argument \(\dfrac{x}{2} \to 0\) as well, and \(\lim_{u \to 0}\dfrac{\sin u}{u} = 1\), so the bracket tends to 1 and \(\lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = \dfrac{1}{4}\). Hence \(k = \dfrac{1}{4}\).

rows.subtopic: Derivatives of Functions in Parametric Form
rows.stem: If \(x = a\cos t\) and \(y = b\sin t\), then find \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\).
rows.solution: Differentiate each parametric equation with respect to the parameter: \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = -a\sin t\) and \(\dfrac{dy}{dt} = b\cos t\). Hence \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} = \dfrac{b\cos t}{-a\sin t} = -\dfrac{b}{a}\cot t\). For the second derivative the step that is easy to lose is that \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) is still a function of \(t\), so it must be differentiated with respect to \(t\) and then multiplied by \(\dfrac{dt}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{dx/dt}\): \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \dfrac{d}{dt}\left(-\dfrac{b}{a}\cot t\right) \cdot \dfrac{dt}{dx} = \dfrac{b}{a}\csc^2 t \cdot \dfrac{1}{-a\sin t}\). Therefore \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = -\dfrac{b}{a^2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sin^3 t}\), which may equally be written \(-\dfrac{b}{a^2}\csc^3 t\).

Work outwards from the innermost function. Since \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) lies in \([-1, 1]\) and the principal value is required, \(\sin^{-1}\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\), so \(2\sin^{-1}\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\). Then \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), so the square bracket becomes \(2 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 1\) and \(\tan^{-1}(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\). The second term is likewise \(\tan^{-1} 1 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\). Adding, the value is \(\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

rows.stem: Show that the determinant \(\begin{vmatrix} x & \sin\theta & \cos\theta \\ -\sin\theta & -x & 1 \\ \cos\theta & 1 & x \end{vmatrix}\) is independent of \(\theta\).
rows.solution: Call the determinant \(\Delta\) and expand along the first row: \(\Delta = x\left[(-x)(x) - (1)(1)\right] - \sin\theta\left[(-\sin\theta)(x) - (1)(\cos\theta)\right] + \cos\theta\left[(-\sin\theta)(1) - (-x)(\cos\theta)\right]\), that is \(\Delta = x(-x^2 - 1) - \sin\theta(-x\sin\theta - \cos\theta) + \cos\theta(-\sin\theta + x\cos\theta)\). Multiplying out, \(\Delta = -x^3 - x + x\sin^2\theta + \sin\theta\cos\theta - \cos\theta\sin\theta + x\cos^2\theta\). The two \(\sin\theta\cos\theta\) terms are equal and opposite, so they cancel; the two remaining \(\theta\) terms combine as \(x(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta) = x\). Hence \(\Delta = -x^3 - x + x = -x^3\). The result contains no \(\theta\) whatsoever, so the determinant is independent of \(\theta\), as required.

rows.stem: Using integration, find the area of the region bounded by \(y = mx\) (m > 0), \(x = 1\), \(x = 2\) and the \(x\)-axis.
rows.solution: Because \(m > 0\), the line \(y = mx\) lies above the x-axis throughout \(x > 0\), so on the strip \(1 \le x \le 2\) the region is the trapezium bounded below by the x-axis, above by \(y = mx\), and at the sides by the vertical lines \(x = 1\) and \(x = 2\). Its vertices are \((1, 0)\), \((2, 0)\), \((2, 2m)\) and \((1, m)\). Integrating with respect to \(x\), Area \(= \displaystyle\int_{1}^{2} mx\,dx = m\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_{1}^{2} = m\left(\dfrac{4}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{3m}{2}\) square units. As a check, the trapezium has parallel sides of length \(m\) and \(2m\) a distance 1 apart, giving \(\dfrac{1}{2}(m + 2m)(1) = \dfrac{3m}{2}\), the same value.

rows.subtopic: Equation of a Line in Space
rows.stem: Find the coordinates of the foot of the perpendicular drawn from point (5, 7, 3) to the line \(\dfrac{x - 15}{3} = \dfrac{y - 29}{8} = \dfrac{z - 5}{-5}\).
rows.solution: Put each of the three equal ratios equal to \(\lambda\). A general point of the line is then \(M(3\lambda + 15,\ 8\lambda + 29,\ -5\lambda + 5)\), and the line's direction ratios are \(3, 8, -5\). With \(P(5, 7, 3)\), the direction ratios of \(PM\) are \((3\lambda + 15 - 5,\ 8\lambda + 29 - 7,\ -5\lambda + 5 - 3) = (3\lambda + 10,\ 8\lambda + 22,\ -5\lambda + 2)\). This general point is the FOOT of the perpendicular for the one value of \(\lambda\) that makes \(PM\) perpendicular to the line, i.e. for which \((3\lambda + 10)(3) + (8\lambda + 22)(8) + (-5\lambda + 2)(-5) = 0\). Expanding, \(9\lambda + 30 + 64\lambda + 176 + 25\lambda - 10 = 0\), so \(98\lambda + 196 = 0\) and \(\lambda = -2\). Substituting back, \(M = (-6 + 15,\ -16 + 29,\ 10 + 5) = (9, 13, 15)\). Checking: \(PM = (4, 6, 12)\) and \(4(3) + 6(8) + 12(-5) = 12 + 48 - 60 = 0\), which confirms the perpendicularity. So the foot of the perpendicular is \((9, 13, 15)\).

rows.stem: If \(\vec{a} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\) and \(\vec{b} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}\) then find a unit vector perpendicular to both \(\vec{a} + \vec{b}\) and \(\vec{a} - \vec{b}\).
rows.solution: First form the two vectors: \(\vec{a} + \vec{b} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\) and \(\vec{a} - \vec{b} = -\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}\). A vector perpendicular to both is their cross product, \(\vec{c} = (\vec{a} + \vec{b}) \times (\vec{a} - \vec{b}) = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 \end{vmatrix}\). Expanding, \(\vec{c} = \hat{i}\left[(3)(-2) - (4)(-1)\right] - \hat{j}\left[(2)(-2) - (4)(0)\right] + \hat{k}\left[(2)(-1) - (3)(0)\right] = -2\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}\). Its magnitude is \(|\vec{c}| = \sqrt{4 + 16 + 4} = \sqrt{24} = 2\sqrt{6}\), so the required unit vector is \(\dfrac{\vec{c}}{|\vec{c}|} = \dfrac{-2\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}}{2\sqrt{6}} = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\hat{i} + \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\hat{j} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\hat{k}\). Its negative, \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\left(\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}\right)\), is perpendicular to both as well and is equally acceptable. As a check, \((\vec{a} + \vec{b}) \times (\vec{a} - \vec{b}) = -2(\vec{a} \times \vec{b})\), and \(\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}\), which reproduces \(\vec{c}\).

rows.subtopic: Graphical Solution and the Feasible Region
rows.stem:
Solve the following Linear Programming Problem graphically :

Minimise : \(Z = 60x + 80y\)

subject to constraints :

\(3x + 4y \ge 8\)

\(5x + 2y \ge 11\)

\(x, y \ge 0\)
rows.solution: Draw the boundary lines \(3x + 4y = 8\) and \(5x + 2y = 11\) in the first quadrant. The origin satisfies neither inequality, so the feasible region is the part of the first quadrant lying away from the origin on both lines; it is UNBOUNDED. Its corner points are: \(B\left(0, \dfrac{11}{2}\right)\), where \(5x + 2y = 11\) meets the y-axis; \(C\left(\dfrac{8}{3}, 0\right)\), where \(3x + 4y = 8\) meets the x-axis; and the intersection of the two lines, found by substituting \(y = \dfrac{11 - 5x}{2}\) into \(3x + 4y = 8\) to get \(3x + 2(11 - 5x) = 8\), i.e. \(-7x = -14\), so \(x = 2\) and \(y = \dfrac{1}{2}\), giving \(A\left(2, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\). Note that \((0, 2)\) and \(\left(\dfrac{11}{5}, 0\right)\) are NOT corners: each satisfies one constraint but violates the other. Evaluating \(Z = 60x + 80y\) at the corners: \(Z_B = 0 + 440 = 440\), \(Z_A = 120 + 40 = 160\), \(Z_C = 160 + 0 = 160\). The smallest corner value is 160, reached at both \(A\) and \(C\). Since the objective line \(60x + 80y = 160\) is \(3x + 4y = 8\) after dividing by 20 — one of the boundary lines itself — the value 160 is taken at every point of the segment \(AC\), not just at its ends. Because the region is unbounded, a smallest corner value is not automatically a minimum, so one further check is needed: \(60x + 80y < 160\) is the same as \(3x + 4y < 8\), and no feasible point can satisfy that, since every feasible point obeys \(3x + 4y \ge 8\). The open half-plane therefore has no point in common with the feasible region, and the minimum genuinely exists. Hence the minimum value of Z is 160, attained at every point of the segment joining \(A\left(2, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\) and \(C\left(\dfrac{8}{3}, 0\right)\). [Note: the marking scheme reaches the same answer but does not print this last open-half-plane check, which an unbounded feasible region requires; it is included above for completeness, not because the scheme's answer is wrong.]
